title: Can You Add a Whole House Dehumidifier to HVAC?
h1: Can You Add a Whole House Dehumidifier to Your HVAC System?
description: Yes, a whole house dehumidifier can be added to most ducted HVAC systems. Learn how it's installed, which homes need one and what to check before you buy.
quick_answer: Yes. A whole house dehumidifier can be added to most ducted HVAC systems. It's usually installed near the air handler or furnace, tied into the return or supply ducts, with its own drain and power. It removes moisture year-round, even when the AC isn't running. Installation involves ductwork, electrical and drainage, so it's a job for a professional.
body:
Most homes with ducted heating and cooling can add a whole house dehumidifier. The unit connects to your existing ductwork, pulls in humid air, removes moisture and sends drier air back through the system to every room. It works alongside your AC and furnace instead of replacing them.

Does a San Diego home really need a dehumidifier?

Many don't. Your air conditioner already removes some moisture while it cools, and much of San Diego County is fairly dry. But some homes do have real humidity problems:

  • Coastal homes where the marine layer keeps indoor air damp for weeks
  • Homes with musty closets, condensation on windows or mildew in bathrooms
  • Homes with an oversized AC that cools fast but shuts off before it can pull out much moisture
  • Houses with crawl spaces or below-grade rooms that stay damp
  • Well-sealed newer homes that trap moisture from showers and cooking
  • Homes with family members whose allergies are triggered by dust mites or mold

During mild spring and fall weather, the AC may barely run, so it isn't removing moisture at all. That's when a dedicated dehumidifier makes the biggest difference.

How is a whole house dehumidifier installed?

The setup depends on your system and where it sits, whether that's the attic, garage or a hall closet. Here's the general process:

  1. Measure and assess. A technician checks humidity levels, the size of the home and the existing ductwork and equipment.
  2. Choose the configuration. Common setups pull air from the return duct and discharge it into the supply duct, or run as a standalone loop with its own ducting.
  3. Mount the unit. It's installed near the air handler, with room for service access.
  4. Connect the ductwork. New duct connections tie the dehumidifier into the system, often with dampers to control airflow.
  5. Add a drain. The removed water needs a path out, usually to an existing condensate line or a separate drain.
  6. Wire it. The unit needs power and a control, either a dedicated humidistat or a thermostat that can manage humidity.
  7. Test and set. The technician confirms airflow, drainage and the humidity setting.

Because the job involves electrical connections and changes to the duct system, it's not a DIY project. Our indoor air quality technicians handle the full installation.

What humidity level should I aim for?

Most health and building guidance points to keeping indoor humidity roughly between 30 and 50 percent. Above that, dust mites, mildew and mold have an easier time. Below that, air can feel dry and irritate your skin and sinuses, which is more of a concern during Santa Ana winds.

A simple hygrometer from a hardware store can tell you where your home sits before you spend anything.

Will a dehumidifier help with mold and musty smells?

It helps prevent them by keeping humidity below the level where mold and mildew grow easily. It won't remove mold that's already growing, though. Existing mold needs to be cleaned up and its moisture source fixed, whether that's a leak, a clogged AC drain or a damp crawl space. Once that's done, steady humidity control keeps it from coming back.

What are the alternatives to a whole house unit?

Before adding equipment, look at the causes. Simpler fixes sometimes solve the problem:

  • Run bathroom fans during showers and for a while after
  • Use the kitchen range hood when cooking, venting outdoors if possible
  • Fix leaks, drainage problems and damp crawl spaces
  • Have the AC checked for proper sizing and airflow settings
  • Use a portable dehumidifier in one problem room

If several rooms are damp, or portable units are running all the time, a whole house unit is usually the cleaner long-term solution.

What maintenance does a whole house dehumidifier need?

Very little. The filter on the unit needs checking and replacing on the manufacturer's schedule, the drain line should be kept clear, and the coil should be looked at during routine HVAC maintenance. Many homeowners have it checked with their yearly tune-up.
faqs: Can a whole house dehumidifier work with any HVAC system?

It works with most ducted systems, including furnaces with AC and ducted heat pumps. Homes with only ductless mini-splits or wall heaters would need a different approach, such as a standalone ducted unit or portable dehumidifiers.
Will a whole house dehumidifier raise my energy bill?
It uses electricity, but drier air often feels cooler, so some homeowners can set the thermostat a bit higher in summer. The overall effect depends on your home and how much the unit runs.
Where does the water go from a whole house dehumidifier?
It drains through a condensate line, usually tied into the existing AC drain or a dedicated drain. There's no bucket to empty.
